chapterTitle: The AI Landscape for Java: Spring AI

parts.partTitle: Why Spring AI Beats Hand-Rolled Clients

beats.headline: Why hand-rolling LLM clients is a liability?
beats.subline: Stop pasting raw JSON. Spring AI brings enterprise-grade orchestration to your JVM services.
beats.narration: Hand-rolling HTTP clients for LLMs is a recipe for disaster. Every provider has different schemas for streaming and tools. Spring AI brings the same portability to AI that Spring Data brought to databases.

beats.title: The Spring AI Abstraction Layer
beats.subtitle: Decoupling business logic from vendor APIs
beats.narration: Your service talks to portable interfaces like ChatClient. Spring AI handles the plumbing, auto-configuration, and vendor-specific serialization. You swap providers by changing a starter, not your business logic.

beats.title: The Fluent ChatClient API
beats.code:
ChatResponse response = chatClient.prompt()
    .system("Review for security bugs.")
    .user(u -> u.text("{code}").param("code", source))
    .call()
    .chatResponse();

steps.explanation: Sets the persona and constraints globally.
Injects dynamic data into prompts safely.

beats.narration: The fluent API makes prompt assembly readable. You define system roles, inject dynamic user content, and execute calls with built-in support for retries and observability.

beats.title: Spring AI vs. LangChain4j
beats.narration: Choose Spring AI if you are already in the Spring ecosystem. It uses familiar patterns like RestClient. If you need framework-agnostic declarative proxies, LangChain4j is your go-to.

beats.title: Part 1 Done
takeaways: Choose based on your framework stack

beats.narration: That covers the architecture. In Part 2, we look at StructuredOutputConverter to turn LLM text into type-safe Java records.

beats.headline: Why parse LLM strings manually?
beats.subline: Stop writing regex for LLM responses. Use StructuredOutputConverter to map AI output directly to Java records.
beats.narration: Stop writing fragile regex to parse LLM responses. Spring AI's StructuredOutputConverter uses Jackson to map AI output directly into your Java records, ensuring type safety at the edge.

beats.title: Strongly Typed AI Responses

steps.explanation: Immutable data carrier for JSON mapping.
Generates schema instructions and parses JSON.

beats.narration: Define a record, call dot entity, and Spring AI does the rest. It injects formatting rules into the prompt and deserializes the JSON response into your object automatically.

beats.title: The Conversion Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From prompt to typed object
beats.narration: The converter acts as a bridge. It tells the model how to format the output before the call, then uses Jackson to safely instantiate your Java record after the response arrives.

beats.title: Managing Dependencies
beats.caption: Use the BOM to avoid version hell

lines.text: Import Spring AI BOM in pom.xml

beats.narration: Always import the Spring AI BOM. It keeps your model starters and vector store dependencies in sync, preventing runtime classpath conflicts between different AI modules.

beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Local LLMs with Ollama →
beats.narration: That's how you keep AI data clean. In Part 3, we move to local development with Ollama to save costs and keep data private.

beats.headline: Why pay for GPT-4 during local testing?
beats.subline: Run quantized models locally with Ollama. It is fast, free, and keeps your data off the cloud.
beats.narration: Why burn API credits during local testing? Ollama lets you run open-weight models like Llama 3 locally. It is fast, free, and keeps your proprietary data within your own machine.

beats.title: Spinning up Ollama
beats.caption: Docker-based local inference

lines.text: docker exec -it ollama ollama pull llama3.2

beats.narration: Spin up the container, pull your model, and you have a local inference engine. Spring AI connects to it via standard HTTP, making it a drop-in replacement for cloud models.

beats.title: Configuring Local Models
beats.code:
spring:
  ai:
    ollama:
      base-url: http://localhost:11434
      chat:
        options:
          model: llama3.2
beats.narration: Just point the base URL to your local port. Use Spring profiles to toggle between cloud providers for production and Ollama for your local dev environment.

beats.title: Cloud vs. Local Strategy
beats.narration: Use cloud models for complex reasoning tasks in production. Use local models for development, integration tests, and scenarios where data privacy is non-negotiable.

beats.title: Part 3 Complete

beats.headline: Is your AI service bleeding money?
beats.subline: Unbounded LLM calls are a financial risk. Monitor tokens and set strict timeouts.
beats.narration: Unbounded LLM calls are a financial risk. A stuck loop can burn thousands of tokens in seconds. You need strict token limits, timeouts, and observability before going to production.

beats.title: Monitoring Token Usage
beats.narration: Always extract usage metadata. Push these counts to Micrometer so you can visualize token spend in Grafana and set alerts if usage spikes unexpectedly.

beats.title: Production Guardrails
beats.subtitle: Protecting your service
beats.narration: Guardrails are non-negotiable. Set token caps to prevent runaway costs, configure strict HTTP timeouts to fail fast, and redact PII to keep your data compliant.

beats.title: Chapter Summary
beats.caption: Mastering the AI landscape
beats.narration: You now have the blueprint for production-ready AI in Java. Use these patterns to build resilient, observable, and cost-effective AI services.
